title: Can We Get This New Teacher a Quick and Meaningful Win?
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Responding to a student teacher who asks for a guidebook to get from drowning to competent, Dan Meyer proposes a five-day, five-to-ten-minute-a-day routine aimed at a quick win that keeps paying off: leading a group discussion. He first explains why discussions go quiet, which is usually that students do not understand the question, cannot answer in a personal way, or cannot find a safe way to answer, rather than a lack of wait time. His routine pairs a short visual (the first act of a 3-Act Math task) with an unforced question and offers students several low-risk ways to respond, from thinking silently to sharing with a neighbour. He adds warm calling and notes the answer can be optional because student thinking matters more in the moment. Colleagues on the Desmos coaching team add advice about greeting students, lowering the bar, seeing potential and noticing bright spots. The post closes by admiring the TeachingWorks description of group discussion as a high-leverage practice.
points: Quiet classes are rarely a wait-time problem; students are usually confused by the question, cannot answer personally, or lack a safe way to answer.
A week of daily visual-plus-question prompts builds the mechanics of discussion so Friday feels easier than Monday.
Offering several response modes (silent thought, writing, neighbour talk, raised hands) makes participation safe and gives the teacher a sense of which structures fit.
Warm calling, in which the teacher tells a student their idea is interesting and asks permission to call on them, brings small-group thinking to the whole class.
The coaching-team advice (greet students at the door, lower your bar, notice bright spots) shows that early wins can be relational as well as technical.
quotes: I would love to offer Josh a way to spend 5-10 minutes every day next week. I’d like that investment of time to start paying off quickly (because new teachers aren’t generally suffering from too many wins) and also continue paying off over time.

The class, collectively, has become smarter in ways that it could not on its own. Students have learned that their classmates and, indeed, they themselves are smarter than they originally thought. Group discussions testify to many of the reasons why we learn math together in a classroom rather than alone in a library.
A group discussion minus the discussion is just a group … staring at you. It’s one of the worst feelings in a teacher’s day.

Your prime directive here is to make sure students understand that you are interested in how they are thinking and, by extension, in them as individuals. They are wondering if you are only interested in hearing a faint echo of your own thinking and your job is to communicate to them, “No, I am interested in yours.
Lower your bar and be kind to yourself. You will mess up, and when you do, apologize to the class. Let them see you as human too.

The purposes of a discussion are to build collective knowledge and capability in relation to specific instructional goals and to allow students to practice listening, speaking, interpreting, agreeing and disagreeing. The teacher and a wide range of students contribute orally, listen actively, and respond to and learn from others’ contributions. Teachers work to ensure students are positioned as competent among their peers, that patterns of interaction are respectful, and that the collective work of the group uses the strengths of and benefits each student.
